#clean and convert "Annual household income"

```{r}
#search the usage of Pseudo_R2 and do.call function in R with chatgpt
#1c
new_data=merge(AUX,DEMO,by="SEQN",all=FALSE)

new_data$gender=factor(
  new_data$RIAGENDR,
  levels=c(1,2),
  labels=c("Male","Female")
)

new_data$citizenship=factor(
  new_data$DMDCITZN,
  levels=c(1,2),
  labels=c("US Citizen","Non-US Citizen")
)

#convert "Number of children" into continuous variable and code as 3 to the households with three or more children
new_data$children=as.numeric(new_data$DMDHHSZA)

#use the middle points of every range in "Annual household income" as its representative value
mid_income=c("1"=2500,
             "2"=7500,
             "3"=12500,
             "4"=17500,
             "5"=22500,
             "6"=30000,
             "7"=40000,
             "8"=50000,
             "9"=60000,
             "10"=70000,
             "14"=87500,
             "15"=125000)
new_data$income=unname(mid_income[as.character(new_data$INDHHIN2)])

new_data$AUXTWIDR[new_data$AUXTWIDR %in% c(555, 777, 888)]=NA
new_data$AUXTWIDL[new_data$AUXTWIDL %in% c(555, 777, 888)]=NA

#model 1R
m1R=glm(
  AUXTWIDR~gender,
  data=new_data,
  family=poisson(link="log")
)

#model 2R
m2R=glm(
  AUXTWIDR~gender+citizenship+children+income,
  data=new_data,
  family=poisson(link="log")
)

# Model 1L
m1L=glm(
  AUXTWIDL~gender,
  data=new_data,
  family=poisson(link="log")
)

# Model 2L
m2L=glm(
  AUXTWIDL~gender+citizenship+children+income,
  data=new_data,
  family=poisson(link="log")
)

#IRR table
#function inputs are the models and their names, with the output of the data.frame including model, variable and their IRR.
get_IRR=function(model,model_name){
  s=summary(model)$coefficients
  data.frame(
    Model=model_name,
    Variable=rownames(s),
    IRR=sprintf(
      "%.3f",exp(s[,1])
    )
  )
}

models_IRR=list(
  get_IRR(m1R,"1R"),
  get_IRR(m2R,"2R"),
  get_IRR(m1L,"1L"),
  get_IRR(m2L,"2L")
)

IRR_table=do.call(
  rbind,models_IRR
)

knitr::kable(
  IRR_table,
  caption="Poisson Regression Results: IRR"
)

#N, Pseudo-R^2 and AIC table
library(pscl)
#function inputs are the models and their names, with the output of the data.frame including model, numbers, Pseudo-R^2 and their AIC.
get_stats=function(model,model_name){
    data.frame(
    Model=model_name,
    N=nobs(model),
    Pseudo_R2=round(pscl::pR2(model)["McFadden"],3),
    AIC=round(AIC(model),1)
  )
}

models_stats=list(
  get_stats(m1R,"1R"),
  get_stats(m2R,"2R"),
  get_stats(m1L,"1L"),
  get_stats(m2L,"2L")
)

stats_table=do.call(
  rbind,models_stats)

knitr::kable(
  stats_table,
  caption="Poisson Regression Results: Statistics"
)
```

```{r}
#1d
s=summary(m2L)$coefficients
IRR=exp(s["genderFemale",1])
p=s["genderFemale",4]
data.frame(IRR=IRR,p_value=p)
```

Since p value is much smaller than 0.05, we reject the null hypothesis that the IRR=1. And because the IRR number is 1.0189, so it indicates that females have a statistically significantly higher predicted mean left-ear tympanometric width than males, by approximately 1.89%.

```{r}
#search the usage of type parameter and update function in R with chatgpt
#control the only variable--gender
d_fit=model.frame(m2L)

pred_data=data.frame(
  gender=factor(c("Male","Female"),
                levels=levels(d_fit$gender)),
  citizenship=factor(
    c("US Citizen","US Citizen"),
    levels=levels(d_fit$citizenship)
  ),
  children=rep(mean(d_fit$children),2),
  income=rep(mean(d_fit$income),2)
)

# Predict left-ear tympanometric width
pred_data$predicted=predict(
  m2L,
  newdata=pred_data,
  type="response"
)
pred_data

#testing
#Model without gender
m2L_null=update(m2L,.~.-gender)

#Likelihood ratio test
anova(m2L_null,m2L,test="Chisq")
```

Since the p value is 1.826e-07, much smaller than 0.001, we reject the null hypothesis that males and females have equal predicted mean left-ear tympanometric widths.

```{r}
#the functions all just the give the answer to the questions.
#2a
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)
library(microbenchmark)
db<-dbConnect(SQLite(),"E://常用软件//sakila_master.db")

#R method
q1_r=function(){
  store=dbGetQuery(db,"SELECT store_id FROM store")
  customer=dbGetQuery(db,"SELECT store_id,active FROM customer")
  
  result=do.call(rbind,lapply(store$store_id,function(id){
    x=customer$active[customer$store_id==id]
    data.frame(
      store_id=id,
      n_customers=length(x),
      active_pct=if(length(x)>0)100*mean(x==1)else NA_real_)
  }))
  
  result$active_pct=round(result$active_pct,2)
  result[order(result$store_id),]
}
q1_r()

#SQL method
q1_sql=function(){
  dbGetQuery(db,"
    SELECT s.store_id,COUNT(c.customer_id) AS n_customers,
    ROUND(100.0*AVG(c.active),2) AS active_pct
    FROM store s
    LEFT JOIN customer c ON s.store_id=c.store_id
    GROUP BY s.store_id
    ORDER BY s.store_id
  ")
}
q1_sql()
```

```{r}
#2b
#R method
q2_r=function(){
  staff=dbGetQuery(db,"SELECT first_name,last_name,address_id FROM staff")
  address=dbGetQuery(db,"SELECT address_id,city_id FROM address")
  city=dbGetQuery(db,"SELECT city_id,country_id FROM city")
  country=dbGetQuery(db,"SELECT country_id,country FROM country")
  
  x=merge(staff,address,by="address_id")
  x=merge(x,city,by="city_id")
  x=merge(x,country,by="country_id")
  
  result=data.frame(
    name=paste(x$first_name,x$last_name),
    country=x$country
  )
  
  result[order(result$name),]
}
q2_r()

#SQL method
q2_sql=function(){
  dbGetQuery(db,"
    SELECT s.first_name||' '||s.last_name AS name,co.country
    FROM staff s
    JOIN address a ON s.address_id=a.address_id
    JOIN city ci ON a.city_id=ci.city_id
    JOIN country co ON ci.country_id=co.country_id
    ORDER BY name
  ")
}
q2_sql()
```

```{r}
#2c
#R method
q3_r=function(){
  payment=dbGetQuery(db,"SELECT rental_id,amount FROM payment")
  rental=dbGetQuery(db,"SELECT rental_id,inventory_id FROM rental")
  inventory=dbGetQuery(db,"SELECT inventory_id,film_id FROM inventory")
  film=dbGetQuery(db,"SELECT film_id,title FROM film")
  
  max_payment=max(payment$amount,na.rm=TRUE)
  payment=payment[payment$amount==max_payment,]
  
  x=merge(payment,rental,by="rental_id")
  x=merge(x,inventory,by="inventory_id")
  x=merge(x,film,by="film_id")
  
  data.frame(title=sort(unique(x$title)))
}
q3_r()

#SQL method
q3_sql=function(){
  dbGetQuery(db,"
    SELECT DISTINCT f.title
    FROM payment p
    JOIN rental r ON p.rental_id=r.rental_id
    JOIN inventory i ON r.inventory_id=i.inventory_id
    JOIN film f ON i.film_id=f.film_id
    WHERE p.amount=(SELECT MAX(amount) FROM payment)
    ORDER BY f.title
  ")
}
q3_sql()
```

```{r}
#micronbenchmark testing
mb1=microbenchmark(R=q1_r(),SQL=q1_sql(),times=100)
mb2=microbenchmark(R=q2_r(),SQL=q2_sql(),times=100)
mb3=microbenchmark(R=q3_r(),SQL=q3_sql(),times=100)

print(mb1)
print(mb2)
print(mb3)
```

No matter which questions, we can always see from the microbenchmark testing that SQL approach has the shorter time and the quicker speed( from mean and median figures).

```{r}
#3d
format_phone=function(x){
  digits=gsub("[^0-9]","",x)
  
  paste0(
    substr(digits,1,4),"-",
    substr(digits,5,7),"-",
    substr(digits,8,10)
  )
}

au$phone1=format_phone(au$phone1)
au$phone2=format_phone(au$phone2)

head(au$phone1,10)
head(au$phone2,10)
```

```{r}
#3e
apt=regmatches(au$address,regexpr("[0-9]+$",au$address))
apt=as.numeric(apt)
apt=apt[!is.na(apt)&apt>0]

hist(log(apt),
     main="Log of Apartment Numbers",
     xlab="Log(Apartment Number)",
     ylab="Frequency")
```

```{r}
#3f
first_digit=as.numeric(substr(as.character(apt),1,1))
observed=table(factor(first_digit,levels=1:9))
observed

Benford=log10(1+1/(1:9))
comparison=data.frame(
  digit=1:9,
  observed=round(as.numeric(prop.table(observed)),3),
  Benford=round(Benford,3)
)
comparison

#Chi-square Test
test=chisq.test(observed,p=Benford)
test
```

We use Chi-square test here to see if the dataset satisfies the Benford's law distribution. Since the p value is 1.67e-10, much smaller than 0.001, we reject the null hypothesis, which means that it doesn't appear to follow the Benford's law. As a real data, apartment numbers always appear to start with 1 or 2, they don't naturally occur, so in my opinion, it may not be expected to follow Benford's law in real data.
